query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of lightweight high-entropy alloys to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance can be explained by the formation of a stable solid solution phase, which is influenced by the high configurational entropy of the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Lightweight high-entropy alloys with a multi-principal element composition
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of alloying elements and their proportions
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions, controlled atmosphere, and mechanical loading
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution phase
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy inhibiting segregation and promoting the formation of a solid solution phase, which enhances mechanical properties and corrosion resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance with decreasing density
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys with a single main element
generation.boundary: Limitations imposed by the single-primary-element design approach, high density, and inadequate mechanical properties
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between alloy composition, microstructure, and properties is not fully understood, and further research is needed to optimize the performance of lightweight high-entropy alloys

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of lightweight high-entropy alloys with varying alloying elements and proportions, tested under high-temperature conditions and mechanical loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the formation of a stable solid solution phase does not correlate with improved mechanical properties and corrosion resistance, the hypothesis is falsified

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) were first proposed and named in 2004 []. It is generally believed that high-entropy alloys have four major effects: a high-entropy effect in thermodynamics, a hysteresis diffusion effect in dynamics, a lattice distortion effect in structure, and a “cocktail” effect in performance. Multiple principal elements have led to higher mixing entropy, which can inhibit segregation and even the combination of elements, thus promoting the formation of solid solutions of single FCC, BCC, and HCP phases [,,]. Due to the diffusion-activated energy and interatomic binding force of different principal element atoms, these factors hinder the diffusion of atoms, making high-entropy alloys stable in a wide temperature range. In addition, the difference in atomic size will inevitably lead to more or less lattice distortion of the alloy, thus affecting its mechanical properties. Finally, the characteristics of different principal elements will interact with each other and influence each other to develop a synergistic performance effect. Conventional alloys have been beaten by HEAs, as demonstrated by extensive research conducted over the past decade. These include the capacity to maintain their structure and properties at elevated temperatures, a robust resistance to microstructural changes, high hardness, and exceptional high-temperature strength. Furthermore, HEAs demonstrate outstanding resistance to high-temperature softening, corrosion, fatigue, and wear []. In contrast to conventional alloys, HEAs are composed of five or more elements, each of which contributes 5–35% to the overall composition []. The design of traditional alloys typically relies on one or two primary elements, with the minor addition of other elements to regulate properties such as strength, ductility, corrosion resistance and so on, such as steel, aluminium alloys and titanium alloys. This single-primary-element design approach inevitably imposes limitations on alloy composition design. In view of this, Yeh proposed the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in 2004 [], which were denoted as multi-principal elements alloys composed of five or more elements, with each element’s content ranging from 5 at.% to 35 at.%. HEAs concept significantly expands the compositional space for alloy design and provides new ideas for the development of novel alloy materials. Compared to traditional alloys, HEAs exhibit a range of exceptional properties, such as outstanding corrosion resistance, remarkable high-temperature strength, and good low-temperature plasticity [,,,,]. These characteristics suggest significant potential for application in fields such as aerospace and marine structures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials that contain multiple principal elements in near-equiatomic ratios. This unique composition results in distinctive structural and mechanical properties. Unlike conventional alloys, which are based on a single main element, HEAs offer high strength, hardness, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties make them attractive for applications in aerospace, defence, and high-temperature environments,. The high configurational entropy in HEAs helps forming a stable solid solutions, which contributes to their exceptional mechanical behaviour. Among various HEAs, the AlCoCrFeNi system has attracted significant interest because of its unique microstructure and mechanical properties. In particular, the Al0.3CoCrFeNi alloy has been widely studied because of its stable face-centred cubic (FCC) structure, which improves properties such as wear resistance and toughness. Increasing the aluminium content leads to a phase transformation from FCC to body-centred cubic (BCC), which significantly affects the hardness and yield strength of the alloy. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), firstly proposed in 2004, have attracted extensive attention due to their outstanding mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, irradiation resistance and thermal stability [,,,,]. HEAs are generally composed of at least five kinds of elements with an atomic percentage between 5% and 35% in equal mole or near equal mole ratios [,]. Differing from conventional alloys, HEAs tend to form simple solid solution structures, such as face-centered cubic (FCC), body-centered cubic (BCC) and close-packed hexagonal (HCP), rather than intermetallic compounds or amorphous phases due to their higher mix entropy [,,,]. However, the existing HEAs also contain several intermetallic compounds, which can strengthen the mechanical properties [,]. Earlier studies have explored the effects of different alloying elements, processing techniques, and microstructural features on the properties of these alloys. Recent studies have also investigated the use of high-entropy alloys in various applications, including aerospace and nuclear systems.
decision.unsolved: The ability to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance in high-entropy alloys remains a significant challenge. While some studies have reported promising results, further research is needed to fully understand the relationships between alloy composition, microstructure, and properties.
